title: IFT-BioSim
text:
A national target is one number. The farms that have to meet it are thousands of different businesses, and the same target can cost one of them very little and another a great deal. IFT-BioSim asks how a common national transition objective can create very different economic pressures across heterogeneous farms.
It focuses on who bears adjustment, who responds, and how policy design changes incidence.

title: Monika Zurek: Can food-system foresight change decisions before crises arrive?
text:
Monika Zurek is an Associate Professor and leader of the Food System Transformation Group at the University of Oxford’s Environmental Change Institute. Her career asks a question that becomes more urgent as food systems face climate, economic and political shocks: can societies use foresight well enough to change course before a crisis forces them to? Oxford describes her work as focused on food-system transformation, agriculture, climate change and the future of food.
Zurek trained in agricultural biology at the University of Hohenheim and completed a PhD in agricultural economics at Justus Liebig University Giessen. Her early career moved across research and international institutions, including CIMMYT, the FAO, the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and climate-policy consulting. That trajectory made scenarios and institutional decision-making central to her work long before food-systems foresight became a widely used policy term.
At Oxford she co-leads Foresight4Food and has worked on the resilience of the UK food system as well as international projects exploring how scenarios, models and participatory processes can support transformation. Recent research has examined sustainability navigation, food-system resilience, governance of transformation and how foresight exercises actually influence institutions.
The method is deliberately mixed. Quantitative models matter, but so do the actors who interpret them, the assumptions that structure future scenarios and the organisations expected to act. Zurek’s current work on the impact of food-system foresight asks not only whether a scenario is scientifically sophisticated but whether it lands in a policy environment in a way that changes choices.
The unresolved problem is that foresight can become theatre. Institutions can run workshops, generate scenarios and still continue along the same path. Zurek’s work pushes toward a harder standard: what evidence would show that anticipating the future genuinely changed present decisions?

Monika Zurek
Associate Professor, University of Oxford
Field: Food systems and environmental change
Research focus: Foresight, resilience, agriculture and climate policy
Training: Agricultural biology; PhD agricultural economics
Current initiative: Foresight4Food

title: Mary Abukutsa-Onyango: What changes when neglected vegetables are treated as serious crops?
text:
Mary Abukutsa-Onyango is Deputy Vice Chancellor for Research, Production and Extension at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and a Professor of Horticulture whose career has been built around African indigenous vegetables. For decades, crops such as African nightshade, spider plant and amaranth were often treated by formal research systems as minor or backward foods despite their nutritional, cultural and agronomic value. Abukutsa-Onyango’s work helped turn that assumption into a research question: what happens when these vegetables receive the same attention given to major commercial crops?
Her route into the problem crossed both public service and universities. She trained in agriculture and agronomy at the University of Nairobi and completed a doctorate in horticultural sciences at the University of London. Before university leadership roles, she worked in Kenya’s Ministry of Agriculture as a district horticultural officer, on cereal crops, agricultural information and horticultural export inspection. JKUAT records a career of more than three decades in public service, research, teaching and extension.
The research has included germplasm collection, agronomy, seed systems, nutritional analysis, processing and the development and promotion of African indigenous vegetable varieties. That breadth is important because neglected crops do not become mainstream through breeding alone. Farmers need seed, consumers need reliable markets, researchers need evidence on nutrition and production, and extension systems have to recognise the crop as worth supporting.
Abukutsa-Onyango has also used institutional leadership to push that agenda. In 2025 she was appointed Editor-in-Chief of the ASRIC Journal of Agricultural Sciences and received the Africa Food Prize for her work on African indigenous vegetables. JKUAT also records her leadership of a Kenyan consortium scaling climate-smart technologies for indigenous vegetables in Kiambu and Kakamega counties. The work now spans research, farmer training, postgraduate capacity building and policy visibility.
The unresolved question is what happens when neglected crops succeed. Commercialisation can expand production and diets, but it can also narrow diversity toward a few marketable varieties or shift control over seed and value chains. The next phase is therefore not merely to convince institutions that indigenous vegetables matter. It is to scale them without losing the genetic diversity, farmer knowledge and nutritional purposes that made them worth recovering in the first place.

Mary Abukutsa-Onyango
Deputy Vice Chancellor (Research, Production and Extension), JKUAT
Field: Horticulture
Research focus: African indigenous vegetables, nutrition and crop diversity
Training: University of Nairobi; PhD Horticultural Sciences, University of London
Recognition: Africa Food Prize, 2025

title: Rachel Wynberg: Who should benefit when biodiversity becomes an economic resource?
text:
Rachel Wynberg is a professor at the University of Cape Town and holder of the South African Research Chair in the Environmental and Social Dimensions of the Bio-economy. Her work starts from a question that becomes more urgent as biological resources gain commercial value: when plants, genes, seeds and traditional knowledge become inputs into new products and industries, who has the right to decide how they are used and who shares the benefits? UCT describes her research as spanning biodiversity-based economies, agroecology, social and environmental justice and alternative agricultural futures.
Wynberg came to the field through both natural and social sciences. She trained in marine biology and environmental policy before moving more deeply into political ecology and governance. Over more than two decades she has advised governments, civil-society organisations, communities and international agencies on biodiversity, access and benefit sharing, seed systems and emerging technologies. That career places her between formal policy institutions and the communities whose knowledge and resources those institutions are trying to regulate.
A major strand of her work concerns access and benefit sharing: the rules that govern how genetic resources and associated knowledge can be used, researched and commercialised. She has also worked on farmers’ rights, agrobiodiversity, seed sovereignty and the social implications of new genetic technologies. Wynberg was a lead author on the IPBES Sustainable Use of Wild Species Assessment, bringing her work into a global process concerned with how wild species can be used without undermining biodiversity or the people who depend on it.
Her current research chair widens the argument. The “bio-economy” can describe very different futures, from biotechnology-intensive growth to locally rooted systems built around agroecology, community rights and ecological limits. Wynberg’s research asks which of those visions is privileged by policy, investment and science, and which are pushed aside. She also supervises postgraduate research and teaches a course on critical perspectives on the bio-economy at UCT.
The unresolved issue is distribution. A biodiversity-based economy can create new markets and scientific opportunities, but it can also reproduce older forms of extraction if communities supply resources or knowledge without meaningful power over how value is created and shared. Wynberg’s work keeps that political question at the centre. The challenge is not simply to build a bio-economy, but to decide what kind of economy it becomes and whether conservation, justice and innovation can be made to reinforce rather than undermine one another.

Rachel Wynberg
Professor and SARChI Research Chair, University of Cape Town
Field: Political ecology and environmental governance
Research focus: Bio-economy governance, biodiversity, justice and benefit sharing
Selected role: Lead author, IPBES Sustainable Use of Wild Species Assessment
Teaching: Critical Perspectives on the Bio-economy

title: Joyce Chitja: What has to change before smallholder farmers can reach better markets?
text:
Joyce Chitja is an Associate Professor at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and Director of its African Centre for Food Security. Her research starts from a problem that often disappears in discussions of agricultural productivity. A smallholder can produce more food and still remain economically insecure if markets, water, institutions and bargaining power prevent that production from becoming a reliable livelihood. UKZN describes her programme as spanning food and nutrition security, water-use security, smallholder development and market access.
Chitja has spent roughly two decades at UKZN, developing a career that combines academic research with community engagement. The distinction is important. Her work is not organised around studying rural communities from a distance and then returning with recommendations. UKZN highlights a commitment to translating research into action, alongside postgraduate supervision, mentoring and regional policy engagement.
Food security in this framing is not simply a question of calories. It is produced by linked systems. Farmers require land and water, but they also need market information, logistics, relationships with buyers and institutions that can reduce the risks of participating in higher-value supply chains. Chitja’s work has examined these connections in smallholder agriculture, particularly where rural development and commercial opportunity meet.
As director of the African Centre for Food Security, she also works across disciplinary boundaries. Food insecurity can reflect agricultural production, income, household decisions, infrastructure and public policy at the same time. The centre’s work therefore creates an institutional setting for research that cannot be solved inside one conventional agricultural discipline. UKZN also records a long history of master’s and doctoral supervision and contributions to food-security policy and programmes in South Africa and the wider SADC region.
The unresolved question is what successful integration into markets should mean. Linking smallholders to a formal value chain can raise income, but it can also expose households to new standards, costs and dependencies. Productivity alone does not settle who captures value or who carries risk. Chitja’s work points toward a broader test: whether market participation improves food security and rural livelihoods on terms that smallholder farmers can sustain.

Joyce Chitja
Associate Professor and Director, African Centre for Food Security, UKZN
Field: Food and nutrition security
Research focus: Smallholder development, market access and water security
Career: About two decades at UKZN
Scientific community: Postgraduate supervision, policy engagement and community-engaged research

title: Leonie Wenz: What does climate change cost society before disaster becomes visible?
text:
Leonie Wenz is Professor of Environmental Economics at Technical University Berlin and leads the Societal Transition and Well-being lab at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. Her research asks how climate change affects economic performance and human welfare, including effects that are dispersed across ordinary days rather than concentrated in headline disasters. PIK describes her programme as quantifying social and economic climate costs to inform resilient development.
Wenz trained in mathematics before completing a PhD at the intersection of climate physics and economics at the University of Potsdam and PIK. She later conducted postdoctoral research at UC Berkeley in natural-resource economics. That combination of mathematical training, climate science and economics shaped a research style built around large datasets and causal inference.
Her work has examined how heat affects labour productivity, economic growth, educational outcomes and social behaviour, and how climate shocks propagate through trade and supply networks. The aim is to estimate damages that conventional disaster accounting can miss. A heatwave does not need to destroy a building to impose economic costs.
Since 2025 Wenz has held a joint TU Berlin–PIK professorship focused explicitly on climate damages and adaptation. Her group studies responses at individual, regional and international scales, using observational data, statistical methods and increasingly machine-learning tools.
The unresolved challenge is attribution and adaptation. Economic outcomes are shaped by many forces at once, while societies adjust to climate over time. Estimating the cost of warming therefore requires separating weather effects from broader trends and understanding which losses can realistically be avoided. Wenz’s work sits at that boundary between identifying damage and measuring society’s capacity to adapt.

Leonie Wenz
Professor of Environmental Economics, Technical University Berlin
Field: Environmental and climate economics
Research focus: Climate damages, adaptation and well-being
Training: Mathematics; PhD Climate Physics/Economics
PIK role: Lab Leader, Societal Transition and Well-being

title: Petra Holden: Can nature-based solutions be both effective and fair?
text:
Petra Holden is a Senior Researcher at the University of Cape Town’s African Climate and Development Initiative and leads the People in Nature & Climate Lab. Her work focuses on nature-based solutions, a phrase that can make environmental interventions sound more straightforward than they are. Restoring vegetation, clearing invasive trees or protecting ecosystems may improve water, biodiversity or climate resilience, but the benefits and costs do not necessarily fall on the same people. ACDI describes her research as explicitly crossing natural and social sciences to examine whether nature-based solutions are both equitable and effective.
Holden trained in conservation biology at the University of Cape Town and worked in restoration consulting and conservation policy before returning to academic research. That trajectory matters because it placed her early in settings where ecological evidence has to survive contact with policy, budgets and local interests. Her current lab uses field studies, modelling, artificial intelligence and synthesis to examine ecosystem-service dynamics, incentives for investment and approaches to co-governance.
One strand of her work looks at hydrology. Clearing invasive alien trees from mountain catchments can restore streamflow, but it can also alter carbon storage, habitat and livelihoods. Another strand examines how conservation evidence itself is produced. A 2024 Conservation Biology paper with colleagues argued for methodological pluralism in constructing counterfactuals, the imagined condition against which conservation outcomes are judged. The point is not technical for its own sake. Different counterfactuals can produce different conclusions about whether an intervention “worked”.
Holden’s recent work also connects nature-based solutions to climate services and co-production. That moves the research from ecological response toward the institutions deciding what information counts and whose priorities are represented. In 2023, her work received both the Frontiers Planet Prize and the AXA XL Climate Water Nexus Award, recognition that reflects a programme combining environmental measurement with questions about equity and implementation.
The unresolved issue is that “win-win” claims can conceal distribution. A project may improve average water availability while creating costs for particular workers, land users or communities. It may deliver carbon benefits while reducing another ecosystem service. Holden’s work keeps attention on how those trade-offs are measured and governed. A nature-based solution is not equitable simply because it uses nature. The harder task is designing evidence and institutions that can show who gains, who loses and whether those outcomes are acceptable.

Petra Holden
Senior Researcher, African Climate and Development Initiative
Field: Conservation science and restoration ecology
Research focus: Nature-based solutions, hydrology, biodiversity and social equity
Lab: People in Nature & Climate Lab
Selected recent work: Methodological pluralism for evidence-based conservation, Conservation Biology (2024)

title: Anna Steynor: Why does good climate information so often fail to change decisions?
text:
Anna Steynor is a Senior Scientist in international climate services at the UK Met Office. Her career has focused on a persistent gap in climate science: producing better information does not guarantee that the information will be used. Forecasts, projections and risk assessments can be technically strong and still fail to influence a planning decision if they arrive at the wrong time, answer the wrong question or are difficult for users to interpret. The Met Office currently lists Steynor in its Climate Services Development team, working on international climate services.
Much of that career was built at the University of Cape Town’s Climate System Analysis Group, where Steynor worked in climate services from the mid-2000s and later led the group’s climate-services work. She trained in climate science at UCT and became increasingly interested in what happens after model output is produced. That moved her research toward the psychology of risk perception, co-production and the design of information that people can use in real institutional settings.
Her work has examined climate-service needs in South Africa and East Africa, city-scale climate projections and the practical meaning of co-production. In this context, co-production means more than asking users what information they want. It involves scientists and decision-makers working together to define the problem, interpret uncertainty and decide what form of evidence is useful. Steynor and collaborators have also studied how to evaluate whether that process actually improves decisions.
The move to the Met Office extends rather than breaks that trajectory. Climate services are increasingly expected to translate national and global climate science into information for governments, infrastructure operators and climate-sensitive sectors. That requires technical expertise, but also judgement about timing, uncertainty and institutional capacity. A beautifully resolved projection is of little value if the decision it was designed to inform has already been made.
The unresolved question is evidence of impact. Co-production is now widely praised, but an inclusive process is not the same as a changed decision. The harder test is whether climate services alter investment, planning or preparedness in ways that reduce risk. Steynor’s work keeps attention on that final step. The success of climate information should not be measured only by whether it was produced or understood, but by whether it became usable enough to change what somebody actually did.

Anna Steynor
Senior Scientist, UK Met Office
Field: Climate services and risk communication
Research focus: Co-production, risk perception and decision-relevant climate information
Earlier career: Climate System Analysis Group, University of Cape Town
Current role: International climate services, Met Office Climate Services Development team

title: Kathryn Fiorella: What happens to nutrition when ecosystems change?
text:
Kathryn Fiorella is an Associate Professor in Cornell University’s Department of Public and Ecosystem Health. Her research examines how environmental change affects human well-being through food systems, livelihoods and nutrition, with a particular focus on fisheries. Cornell identifies planetary health, fisheries, livelihoods and nutrition among her core research areas.
Fiorella trained in ecology and evolutionary biology at Princeton before completing both an MPH and a PhD in Environmental Science, Policy and Management at the University of California, Berkeley. That combination of epidemiology and environmental science shaped a research programme that treats ecological change as a public-health issue rather than a separate environmental problem.
Her work often focuses on fishing communities where aquatic ecosystems provide both food and income. Changes in fish populations can therefore affect diets, household economies and health at the same time. Fiorella uses interdisciplinary methods to trace those links, combining ecological data with household and health information.
This approach is especially relevant in regions where fisheries are under pressure from climate change, overexploitation and shifting markets. A decline in catch does not translate mechanically into one health outcome. Households may change diets, labour, migration or income sources, producing effects that differ across gender and wealth groups.
The unresolved challenge is to identify interventions that protect both ecosystems and people. Restricting fishing may improve ecological recovery while reducing short-term food access. Expanding markets may increase income while accelerating extraction. Fiorella’s work asks how conservation and public health can be designed together rather than forcing communities to choose between them.

Kathryn Fiorella
Associate Professor, Cornell University
Field: Planetary health and environmental epidemiology
Research focus: Fisheries, livelihoods, nutrition and environmental change
Training: PhD and MPH, UC Berkeley
Current role: Food Systems and Health lead, Cornell MPH

title: Yukiko Hashida: How should communities adapt when land itself is changing?
text:
Yukiko Hashida is an Associate Professor in Agricultural and Applied Economics at the University of Georgia. Her research examines how households, landowners and communities respond when climate change alters the value, risk and physical condition of land. Her research profile highlights climate adaptation, land-use change, ecosystem-service valuation, natural disasters and managed retreat.
Hashida’s work sits at the intersection of environmental risk and economic decision-making. Climate adaptation is often described as an engineering problem, but many of the most consequential choices are about whether to remain, relocate, conserve, insure or change how land is used. Those choices depend on incentives, property values, public policy and the distribution of costs.
Her research includes work on coastal adaptation and tidal marshes, where sea-level rise can threaten both ecosystems and private property. In such settings, protecting one asset may reduce another. A seawall can defend buildings while constraining marsh migration. Managed retreat can preserve ecological function while imposing major costs on households and local governments.
Hashida uses applied economic methods to estimate these trade-offs and evaluate adaptation policies. The questions are inherently spatial because the benefits and costs of land-use decisions spill across property boundaries and over time. What one landowner does can affect flood protection, habitat and future development options for others.
The unresolved issue is political feasibility. Economic analysis can identify policies that reduce expected losses or protect ecosystem services, but retreat and land-use restrictions affect wealth, identity and local tax bases. Hashida’s work asks how adaptation can be designed when the economically efficient choice is also socially difficult.

Yukiko Hashida
Associate Professor, University of Georgia
Field: Environmental and resource economics
Research focus: Climate adaptation, land use and managed retreat
Methods: Applied environmental economics and policy analysis
Current themes: Coastal adaptation and ecosystem services

title: Martine Visser: Can behavioural economics change how a city uses scarce water?
text:
Martine Visser is Professor in the School of Economics at the University of Cape Town, Director of the Environmental Policy Research Unit and holder of a research chair in the governance and economics of ecological infrastructure. Her work asks how people behave when environmental resources are shared, scarce and politically difficult to manage. Water provides the clearest example. During Cape Town’s long period of water stress, Visser and collaborators used behavioural economics not simply to describe conservation choices but to test whether carefully designed information could change them.
The intellectual route into economics was not direct. UCT has described Visser as beginning in geology before becoming increasingly interested in sustainable development, livelihoods and the social institutions surrounding environmental problems. She later trained in economics and completed a PhD at the University of Gothenburg. Her publication record was already dealing with environmental policy and collective action by the mid-2000s, including work on South Africa’s plastic-bag legislation and experimental studies of cooperation.
Cape Town turned those interests into a city-scale policy experiment. UCT’s behavioural economics research unit records a randomised controlled trial involving about 400,000 households. Behavioural messages were included with municipal bills for six months. Some compared a household’s water consumption with its neighbourhood; others framed the financial loss from failing to conserve. The study was followed by work with the city on transferring behavioural-insights capacity into local government.
Visser’s research has since broadened beyond individual nudges. Her current chair examines how catchments, rivers, wetlands and other forms of ecological infrastructure can be governed and financed under conditions of inequality, climate risk and scarcity. UCT describes a programme combining field experiments, household and administrative data, cost-benefit analysis and socio-economic modelling. The central concern is not merely how to attach a price to nature, but how institutions can create arrangements that people regard as effective and fair.
That shift also reveals the limitation of behavioural interventions. A message on a bill can influence behaviour, particularly during a visible crisis. It cannot repair a leaking network, create new water supply or resolve deep inequalities in access. The long-term question is therefore how much behaviour can carry and where infrastructure and institutions must take over. Visser’s career sits precisely at that boundary, between the choices individuals make and the systems that determine what choices are possible.

Martine Visser
Professor, University of Cape Town
Field: Behavioural and environmental economics
Research focus: Water, collective action, climate risk and ecological infrastructure
Early publication anchor: Environmental policy and collective-action work, 2006–2007
Major field experiment: Cape Town water-conservation RCT, about 400,000 households

title: Lucy Amissah: How do you manage wildfire without separating forests from the people who live with fire?
text:
Lucy Amissah is Deputy Director and Principal Research Scientist at the CSIR-Forestry Research Institute of Ghana. Her work has followed fire through forests, farms and communities for more than two decades. Wildfire is an ecological disturbance, but in Ghana it is also a livelihood, governance and land-management problem. Fire may be used deliberately in farming or landscape management and may also escape into forests and settlements. CSIR-FORIG identifies Amissah as a specialist in tropical forest ecology, forest fire management, biodiversity conservation and forest landscape restoration.
Her career developed from forest ecology into increasingly applied fire-management work. CSIR records research by Amissah on climate change and tree regeneration as early as 2010, while later projects have examined how forests recover from disturbance and how community institutions can reduce wildfire risk. The institution’s 2026 profile of her emphasises a shift from scientific evidence into practical guidance, partnerships and community resilience.
Community-based fire management is central to that work. It includes awareness, fire belts, prescribed burning, volunteer fire brigades and locally organised responses during fire seasons. In 2026 the International Tropical Timber Organization highlighted Amissah’s role in Ghana and her contribution to international integrated-fire-management work. The underlying idea is that fire cannot be managed effectively by treating people solely as a source of ignition. Communities are also part of prevention, detection and response.
At the same time, Amissah remains a forest ecologist. Her recent collaborative research examines how young secondary tropical forests recover structure, diversity, soils and ecosystem functions after disturbance. A 2026 Forest Ecology and Management paper compared recovery in dry and wet secondary forests, while wider collaborations investigate succession across tropical landscapes. This connects fire management to a larger question about what happens after disturbance and how restoration should be judged.
The unresolved problem is that suppression, livelihoods and ecosystem recovery do not always point in the same direction. Preventing destructive wildfire is essential, but fire is also embedded in land-use systems and some ecosystems. Policies imposed without local knowledge can shift rather than solve risk. Amissah’s work therefore treats fire management as both ecological science and collective action: how to reduce destructive fire while building institutions that communities can actually sustain.

Lucy Amissah
Deputy Director and Principal Research Scientist, CSIR-FORIG
Field: Tropical forest ecology
Research focus: Wildfire management, biodiversity and forest restoration
Experience: More than two decades in forestry research and development
Recent research: Secondary tropical forest recovery and ecosystem succession, 2026

title: Jenny Aker: Does more information change how rural markets work?
text:
Jenny Aker is the Daniel G. Sisler Professor of Development Economics at Cornell University. Her research focuses on how information and digital technologies affect economic outcomes in low-income settings, particularly across agricultural markets, education, financial inclusion and social protection. Cornell describes her work as centred on economic development in Africa and the role of information technology in shaping markets and livelihoods.
Aker’s route into research was unusually grounded in development practice. Before completing her PhD in agricultural economics at the University of California, Berkeley, she worked for Catholic Relief Services in West and Central Africa. That experience shaped a career built around field research rather than abstract models alone.
Her best-known work has examined mobile phones, market information and price dispersion in rural Africa. The core mechanism is simple: when farmers, traders and consumers know more about prices and buyers, search costs fall and bargaining conditions can change. But Aker’s later research has complicated the early optimism around digital technology. Access to a phone or digital service does not automatically improve welfare if infrastructure, trust, liquidity or market structure remain binding constraints.
She has conducted fieldwork across a wide range of African countries and has studied technology adoption, food markets, social protection and digital financial services. Her current roles also include leadership in J-PAL’s Digital Identification and Finance Initiative in Africa.
The unresolved question is when information becomes economically transformative. Better information can reduce friction, but it cannot create roads, storage, credit or competition. Aker’s work therefore asks where digital tools genuinely relax constraints and where they merely make existing constraints more visible.

Jenny Aker
Daniel G. Sisler Professor of Development Economics, Cornell University
Field: Development economics
Research focus: Information technology, agricultural markets and financial inclusion
Training: PhD Agricultural and Resource Economics, UC Berkeley
Fieldwork: Extensive across sub-Saharan Africa

title: Jessica Duncan: Who gets to decide what a sustainable food system looks like?
text:
Jessica Duncan is Associate Professor in the Politics of Food Systems Transformations in Wageningen University’s Rural Sociology Group. Her research begins from a problem that can disappear inside technical discussions of sustainability: who gets to define the problem, choose the evidence and decide what a transformed food system should become? Wageningen describes her work as focusing on participation in food governance and on the possibilities that food policies create, or close down, for just and sustainable transformation.
Duncan completed a PhD in Food Policy at City University London in 2014. Her 2015 book, Global Food Security Governance, examined civil-society engagement in the reformed UN Committee on World Food Security. That institutional setting is important to the career because it turns abstract words such as participation and inclusion into observable processes. Who is invited into a negotiation? Whose language survives into an agreed text? What happens to concepts such as food sovereignty or resilience when they move from social movements into formal governance?
Her methods are therefore different from those of a laboratory scientist, but no less empirical. Duncan works through policy documents, institutions, participant accounts and comparative analysis to follow how power operates through food governance. A 2018 paper with Priscilla Claeys in Food Security examined the opportunities and opposition created by participation in food-security governance. More recent work has looked at knowledge pluralisation in organic agriculture and at the gendered effects of the European Union’s Common Agricultural Policy.
Teaching is unusually visible in her public record. Duncan was Wageningen’s Teacher of the Year in 2017, was shortlisted again in 2018 and 2019 and used award funding to develop storytelling training for students. Wageningen’s research portal also shows her supervising doctoral research on food-system transitions, urban food commons, the Common Agricultural Policy and agency in food systems. That matters because her work is partly about whose knowledge is recognised, and teaching becomes another place where those questions are practised.
The unresolved tension is that participation can be both meaningful and insufficient. Bringing civil society, farmers or marginalised groups into a process does not automatically give them decision power. Institutions can broaden consultation while leaving underlying authority untouched. Duncan’s research keeps that distinction visible. Sustainable food policy is not only a matter of finding the technically best intervention. It is also a question of who can define what “best” means and whose costs, knowledge and priorities are allowed into the decision.

Jessica Duncan
Associate Professor, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Food governance and rural sociology
Research focus: Participation, policy and just food-system transformation
Selected book: Global Food Security Governance (Routledge, 2015)
Teaching: Wageningen Teacher of the Year, 2017

title: Louise Slater: Can flood risk be predicted when the climate itself is changing?
text:
Louise Slater is Professor of Hydroclimatology at the University of Oxford and leads the Hydro-Climate Extremes research group. Her work centres on a forecasting problem made harder by climate change: how can past observations help predict floods and droughts when the statistical behaviour of the system is itself shifting? Oxford lists her research as focused on changing water and weather extremes globally.
Slater’s group develops computational methods that combine river records, Earth observation, climate-model output and machine learning. The aim is not simply to produce a better flood map. It is to identify the physical and climatic drivers of extremes and understand how those drivers vary across space and time.
Her UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship supports the DRIFT project, which integrates observations and modelling to improve understanding of river-flood risk under climate change. The work involves close interaction with agencies responsible for forecasting and flood management, including the Environment Agency, the Flood Forecasting Centre, the Met Office and international hydrological organisations.
The research is increasingly consequential because conventional design assumptions depend on stationarity, the idea that the statistical past remains a reasonable guide to the future. Climate change weakens that assumption. A flood considered rare under twentieth-century records may become much less rare, while land use and infrastructure alter exposure at the same time.
The unresolved question is how much confidence decision-makers can place in projections of extremes. Models can estimate changing probabilities, but local flood risk also depends on catchment condition, infrastructure and human choices. Slater’s work therefore sits between physical prediction and practical uncertainty, trying to make changing risk measurable enough to act on without pretending that the future can be known precisely.

Louise Slater
Professor of Hydroclimatology, University of Oxford
Field: Hydroclimatology
Research focus: Floods, droughts and climate extremes
Research group: Hydro-Climate Extremes
Current programme: DRIFT / UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship

title: Franziska Klein: Can a low-carbon transition also improve well-being?
text:
Franziska Klein is an Assistant Professor at Wageningen University & Research whose work examines the relationship between economic activity, human well-being and environmental pressure. Wageningen describes her background as environmental economics combined with a strong interest in post-growth, ecological and feminist economics.
Klein’s research begins from a problem conventional transition modelling can miss. A low-carbon pathway may reduce emissions while distributing costs unevenly, increasing insecurity or relying on assumptions about growth and consumption that are rarely examined directly. She therefore studies not only whether transitions are technically possible, but how they affect welfare, institutions and power.
Her current projects include European and Dutch research on accelerating just low-carbon transitions. Methodologically, she works across quantitative and qualitative approaches, including econometrics, agent-based modelling and social-ecological systems analysis. That mixed toolkit reflects the fact that justice questions cannot be answered by emissions accounting alone.
The heterodox dimension is important. Ecological economics asks whether economic systems can remain within environmental limits, while feminist economics draws attention to unpaid work, care and distributional effects that standard indicators often overlook. Klein uses these traditions to question what counts as success in a transition.
The unresolved issue is measurement. Climate policy is usually assessed through emissions, GDP, investment or technology deployment. Well-being and justice are harder to summarise, especially when gains for one group coincide with losses for another. Klein’s work asks whether transition analysis can incorporate those outcomes without turning them into vague add-ons.

Franziska Klein
Assistant Professor, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Environmental and ecological economics
Research focus: Just transitions, well-being and political economy
Methods: Econometrics, agent-based modelling and mixed methods
Current projects: ELEVATE, AdJUST and Dutch climate-transition research

title: Siera Vercillo: Who gets to define a just food-system transformation?
text:
Siera Vercillo is an Assistant Professor in Wageningen University’s Public Administration and Policy Group. She describes herself as a scholar-activist, and that position is central to the work rather than incidental to it. Wageningen describes her research as grounded in feminist geography, political ecology and critical development studies, with more than a decade of work in northern Ghana.
Vercillo studies agrarian change, food insecurity, gender and food sovereignty. Her research has examined how rural households diversify livelihoods, how migration reshapes agricultural futures and how global or national policy rules affect smallholder farmers. Recent work includes research on gender disparities in rural livelihood diversification and contestation around seed legislation in Ghana.
Her method is participatory and community-driven. Instead of treating farmers only as respondents, projects are designed with civil-society and food-movement partners and often aim to produce usable change alongside academic analysis. Current work with the Ghana Food Movement, for example, explores neglected and underutilised foods and how culinary practice can support more resilient food systems.
Teaching mirrors that politics of knowledge. Vercillo has developed courses on food sovereignty, gender, cities and development, and currently teaches governance, sustainability practice and research design. Her public profile makes clear that the research is explicitly concerned with rights, power and whose knowledge counts in agricultural policy.
The unresolved tension is between participation and institutional power. Community-led research can reveal alternatives, but governments, donors and markets still control many of the rules shaping seeds, land and food trade. Vercillo’s work asks whether participatory research can do more than document those inequalities and actually change the institutions that reproduce them.

Siera Vercillo
Assistant Professor, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Political ecology and food governance
Research focus: Food sovereignty, gender, agroecology and participatory action research
Long-term field setting: Northern Ghana
Current partner work: Ghana Food Movement

title: Maura Farrell: Who gets to shape the future of rural Europe?
text:
Maura Farrell is Professor of Rural and Agricultural Geography at the University of Galway. Her work examines how rural places change and who gets to participate in deciding what that change should look like. Land use, agricultural restructuring, migration, farm succession, rural youth and gender all enter the picture. Galway’s current profile places a particular emphasis on women as innovators in agriculture and rural life, using gender as a way to understand broader transformations in rural economies and institutions.
The present-day centrepiece is FLIARA, the €3 million Horizon Europe project Farrell coordinates across ten countries. The project studies female-led innovation in agriculture and rural areas through case studies, interviews and collaboration across European research and rural networks. Its premise is deceptively simple. Innovation is often counted through technologies, patents, investment or high-growth firms. Rural change also happens through new forms of care, food production, cooperation, services, community organisation and farm diversification, activities in which women’s contributions can be substantial but less visible to conventional innovation measures.
That question did not appear suddenly with FLIARA. Farrell’s earlier research covered agricultural change, return migration, rural regeneration, forestry, farm families and succession. Work recorded by Galway from the late 2000s onward shows an accumulating concern with how social and spatial inequalities shape rural development. More recent publications have addressed spatial justice, rural sustainability, collaboration in organic farming and participatory governance.
Her research style is correspondingly collaborative. Farrell has led or participated in European projects designed around co-production with stakeholders rather than treating rural communities solely as subjects of study. She is also principal investigator at Galway for PREMIERE, a Horizon Europe project focused on participatory governance and stakeholder engagement. Galway records extensive undergraduate and postgraduate teaching and two nominations for the university’s President’s Award for Teaching Excellence.
The unresolved issue is partly one of recognition. Policy institutions tend to see the forms of innovation they already know how to measure. If rural transformation is evaluated mainly through technological adoption or business growth, other changes can remain institutionally invisible even when they sustain communities or create new livelihoods. Farrell’s work asks what rural policy looks like when those contributions are made visible. The question is not whether rural Europe will change. It is whose innovations, constraints and ideas are allowed to define what a successful rural future becomes.

Maura Farrell
Professor, University of Galway
Field: Rural and agricultural geography
Research focus: Gender, rural development, innovation and spatial justice
Current programme: FLIARA, Horizon Europe
Teaching: Undergraduate and postgraduate rural and agricultural geography

title: Dorcas Kalele: How do climate-smart ideas become decisions farmers can actually use?
text:
Dorcas Kalele is a Kenyan researcher and practitioner working across climate adaptation, agriculture and rural development. Her career sits in a space where conventional institutional labels are often too narrow. She has designed and implemented research and development programmes with universities, international organisations and development agencies, while focusing on how climate evidence becomes policy, investment and changes in farming practice. PlanAdapt describes her work as building a stronger science-policy-practice interface for sustainable food systems and climate-resilient futures.
Kalele’s experience spans more than fifteen years and includes work with organisations such as FAO, the World Bank, GIZ, the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, SNV and other development partners. Current professional profiles also identify her with African research and capacity-building networks concerned with agriculture, food and nutrition security. The thread connecting these roles is not a particular crop or climate model. It is the process through which institutions decide which adaptation practices to support and how those practices reach communities.
Her work focuses on climate-smart agriculture, food-system transformation, rural policy and the inclusion of gender and social differences in adaptation. That last element matters because the category “farmer” hides unequal access to land, finance, information and decision-making. A technology may be climate-resilient in agronomic terms while remaining inaccessible to the people most exposed to climate risk.
Kalele has therefore worked through transdisciplinary and capacity-strengthening approaches rather than treating knowledge transfer as one-way extension. Her involvement in international programmes and climate-research knowledge brokering reflects a recurring concern with context-specific evidence. The same adaptation label can mean very different things across dryland farming, irrigated systems or mixed rural livelihoods.
The unresolved question is implementation. Climate-smart agriculture has accumulated a large menu of practices and technologies, but adoption is shaped by institutions, finance, gender, infrastructure and local priorities. The hard problem is not generating another list of promising options. It is learning which combinations are feasible in a particular place, who is able to adopt them and whether public investment can support adaptation without deepening existing inequalities.

Dorcas Kalele
Climate adaptation and agricultural-development researcher, Kenya
Field: Climate adaptation and rural development
Research focus: Climate-smart agriculture, food systems, gender and policy
Experience: More than 15 years across research and development programmes
Approach: Transdisciplinary research and science-policy-practice translation

title: Anne Mullen: Can food-system climate policy improve nutrition at the same time?
text:
Anne Mullen is a nutrition scientist and lecturer in Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security at the University of Galway. Her present research asks how food systems can reduce environmental pressures while improving nutrition and giving households and citizens a meaningful role in the transition. The question is broad, but her route into it was not. Mullen trained in molecular nutrition at Trinity College Dublin and then worked on complementary feeding for HIV-exposed infants in Zambia, placing nutrition inside a setting where biological need, household conditions and health systems could not be separated. Her Galway biography traces the career from this early public-health work to food-system research.
From 2005 to 2014 she worked as a researcher and lecturer at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and King’s College London. Her work included HIV lipodystrophy and interventions addressing acute malnutrition among HIV-positive children and adults in Uganda. The next move was unusual for an academic trajectory. Mullen became Director of Nutrition at the Dairy Council for Great Britain, where the job centred on translating evidence for citizens, health professionals, researchers, industry and policymakers.
In 2019 she moved again, this time into scientific publishing as the launch Chief Editor of Nature Food. The role placed her at the point where food science, agriculture, nutrition and policy arguments meet. During 2021 and 2022 she organised or moderated discussions connected to the UN Food Systems Summit Science Days, the FAO Science and Innovation Forum, Nutrition for Growth and the International Congress of Nutrition. She returned to university research at Galway in January 2023.
That career makes her present research easier to understand. Mullen studies nutrition security and sustainable food systems, with particular interest in household and citizen agency. She is involved in international programmes examining nutrition and food-system change across countries in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Galway currently lists teaching across food systems, climate change, agriculture, nutrition, global health and gender. Rather than treating communication as an activity that happens after research, her career suggests that the movement of evidence between scientists, citizens, industry and government is itself part of the problem.
The unresolved question is institutional. Governments can write targets for emissions, dietary change or food security. It is harder to specify what households are realistically expected to do, which choices they actually control and how environmental objectives interact with nutrition and affordability. Mullen’s work sits in that gap. Food-system transformation can be modelled at national scale, but it is ultimately lived through meals, shopping decisions, public services and the unequal capacity of households to change.

Anne Mullen
Lecturer, University of Galway
Field: Nutrition and sustainable food systems
Research focus: Nutrition security, citizen agency and food-system transformation
Career path: Public-health nutrition → science communication → Nature Food → University of Galway
Current teaching: Food systems, climate change, agriculture, nutrition and global health

title: Hale Ann Tufan: Who gets designed into a crop-improvement programme?
text:
Hale Ann Tufan is an Associate Professor in Cornell University’s School of Integrative Plant Science and leads the Equitable Agricultural Research Lab. Her work asks a question that plant breeding has often treated as external to biology: who is the crop being improved for? Cornell describes her programme as developing methods that bring gender equality and social inclusion into agricultural research itself.
Tufan’s training spans molecular plant-pathogen interactions, plant breeding, agricultural research management and gender analysis. She has worked with international crop-improvement programmes, including cassava and other staple crops in sub-Saharan Africa. That experience exposed a recurring problem. Breeding programmes can optimise for traits that look valuable in trials while overlooking differences in labour, processing, market access or household decision-making that shape whether farmers actually value a variety.
Her lab works with breeders, social scientists and research institutions to build gender analysis into priority setting, trait selection and evaluation. Tufan has held leadership roles in the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Crop Improvement, the GREAT project and NextGen Cassava, among others. The scientific intervention is therefore partly methodological: changing the questions asked before crosses are made and trials are designed.
That approach challenges the idea that inclusion belongs at the end of a breeding pipeline. If women and marginalised farmers are considered only during adoption studies, many design choices have already been fixed. Tufan’s work moves social evidence upstream.
The unresolved challenge is institutional. Research systems reward measurable genetic gain and yield improvement more easily than equity. Inclusive breeding therefore requires not only better tools but changes in incentives, budgets and professional norms. Tufan’s work asks whether agricultural research can make those changes without treating inclusion as an optional extra.

Hale Ann Tufan
Associate Professor, Cornell University
Field: Plant breeding and gender-responsive agricultural research
Research focus: Inclusive crop improvement and seed systems
Lab: Equitable Agricultural Research (EQUAL) Lab
Major programmes: GREAT, NextGen Cassava, Feed the Future Crop Improvement

title: Hannah van Zanten: What should livestock do in a circular food system?
text:
Hannah van Zanten is a professor at Wageningen University & Research whose work asks what a food system would look like if animals were used only where they add something people cannot obtain more efficiently from crops. Wageningen describes her research as focused on circular food systems that secure human and planetary health.
Van Zanten trained in animal sciences at Wageningen and completed a PhD on the environmental benefits of feeding livestock with resources that humans cannot eat. That question became the foundation of a broader research programme. Instead of asking whether livestock should simply increase or decrease, she asks what ecological role animals can play within a system designed to minimise competition for land and edible biomass.
Her team developed the Circular Food Systems model, or CiFoS, which lets researchers and stakeholders explore combinations of diets, crops, livestock and waste streams. In this framework, livestock can convert grass, crop residues and food-system by-products into food while manure can return nutrients to soils. But animals become inefficient when they consume crops that people could eat directly.
The approach has helped shift debate away from simple comparisons between plant-based and animal-based foods toward whole-system questions about land, nutrient cycles and unavoidable biomass. Van Zanten has also contributed to global work on healthy and sustainable diets and collaborates internationally, including as a visiting professor at Cornell University.
The unresolved issue is how circularity works outside the model. Real supply chains, consumer preferences, regional specialisation and farm economics may resist the system-level optimum. The challenge is therefore not only to identify a theoretically efficient role for livestock, but to understand how existing food systems could move toward it without displacing environmental costs elsewhere.

Hannah van Zanten
Professor, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Farming systems ecology
Research focus: Circular food systems, livestock and planetary health
Training: MSc Animal Sciences; PhD Wageningen
Key model: CiFoS, Circular Food Systems

title: Jill Farrant: Can resurrection plants teach crops to survive drought?
text:
Jill Farrant is a professor in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of Cape Town and holds a South African Research Chair focused on plant desiccation tolerance and food security. Her scientific problem is unusually easy to state and unusually difficult to solve. Most crop plants are damaged irreversibly when their tissues lose too much water. A small group of so-called resurrection plants can dry almost completely, remain in that state for long periods and recover after water returns. Farrant’s career has been devoted to understanding how that survival is possible and what parts of it, if any, can be transferred to crops. UCT describes the aim of her programme as building a fundamental understanding of vegetative desiccation tolerance before deciding what is required for improved crop tolerance.
The question predates the current language of climate-smart agriculture. Farrant completed her postgraduate training at the University of Natal, now the University of KwaZulu-Natal, where her doctoral work examined why recalcitrant seeds are damaged by drying. An early publication anchor is a 1989 Planta paper with Norman Pammenter and Patricia Berjak on germination and desiccation sensitivity in Avicennia marina. UCT’s 2025 account of her career records subsequent research experience in the United States before she moved to Cape Town, where the problem gradually expanded from seeds to the vegetative tissues of resurrection plants. UCT reports more than 250 articles and 18 book chapters.
At the Plant Stress Lab, the work is not a search for one drought-resistance gene. Farrant’s group studies species including Myrothamnus flabellifolia, Xerophyta and resurrection grasses using physiology, biochemistry and high-throughput measurements of transcripts, proteins and metabolites. The lab’s own description stresses that desiccation tolerance involves many interacting genes and protective processes. Its current publication list includes 2025 multi-omics work on Eragrostis nindensis and a 2026 genome assembly of Myrothamnus flabellifolia. The long-running collaborations listed by the lab span South Africa, Europe, Australia, the United States and Zambia.
That continuity matters more than the awards, although the recognition is substantial. Farrant received the L’Oréal-UNESCO Award for Women in Science in 2012 and the NRF Lifetime Achievement Award in 2025. UCT also records a long record of student supervision and research leadership. The more revealing measure of the career is that the same biological problem has survived several generations of techniques. A question first approached through seed physiology can now be examined through genomes and metabolomes.
The difficult part remains translation. Resurrection plants can survive extraordinary water loss, but crop plants must also grow quickly and produce useful yields. Desiccation tolerance appears to depend on coordinated systems with energetic and developmental costs. The challenge is therefore not simply to make maize or wheat survive drought. It is to identify which protective mechanisms can be introduced without giving up the productivity that makes a crop worth growing.

Jill Farrant
Professor, University of Cape Town
Field: Plant molecular biology
Research focus: Desiccation tolerance and food security
Early publication anchor: Farrant, Pammenter & Berjak, Planta (1989)
Recent work: Multi-omics and genome-level studies of resurrection plants, 2025–2026

title: Rachel Bezner Kerr: What changes when farmers become researchers too?
text:
Rachel Bezner Kerr is Professor of Global Development at Cornell University and Director of Cornell’s Institute for African Development. For more than two decades, much of her research has been rooted in northern Malawi and, later, Tanzania. The distinctive feature is not simply that the work studies farmers. It is that farmers and local organisations are treated as participants in producing the knowledge. Cornell describes her approach as long-term, community-based and participatory, combining agriculture, nutrition, ecology and social science.
An early publication anchor is a 2005 Journal of Southern African Studies paper examining food security, gender, kinship and entitlements in northern Malawi. Those concerns remain visible in later work, even as the methods and scale expanded. Bezner Kerr completed a PhD in Development Sociology at Cornell, taught at the University of Western Ontario from 2006 to 2012 and returned to Cornell in 2012. Her long-term collaboration with the Soils, Food and Healthy Communities initiative in Malawi reaches back to around 2000.
The research does not reduce agroecology to a yield experiment. Projects have tested legume intercropping and other agroecological practices while following outcomes such as soil management, household food security, child nutrition, labour and gender relations. That creates a more demanding standard of success. A farming practice can raise yields and still fail if it increases labour burdens, shifts control over food or cannot be sustained without unusually intensive support. Bezner Kerr’s collaborations with farmers, local organisations, public-health researchers and ecologists are therefore part of the method, not decoration around it.
Her publication record now exceeds 100 peer-reviewed papers, chapters and books according to Cornell. She was a Coordinating Lead Author for the food-systems chapter of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report and co-authored the 2019 High Level Panel of Experts report on agroecology. Recent work continues to examine how agroecology is framed across Africa, how gender-transformative interventions affect autonomy and how seed systems interact with food sovereignty and agricultural policy.
The strength of this model is also its complication. Participatory research works partly because relationships, trust and local knowledge accumulate over years. Those conditions cannot be reproduced by simply issuing a national programme and expecting the same result. The question behind Bezner Kerr’s work is therefore larger than whether agroecology works. It is how research, farming knowledge and public policy can be organised so that the people expected to live with a transition help determine what is tested, what counts as success and what is scaled.

Rachel Bezner Kerr
Professor, Cornell University
Field: Agroecology and development
Research focus: Food security, nutrition, gender and participatory research
Early publication anchor: Food security, gender and kinship in northern Malawi, Journal of Southern African Studies (2005)
Long-running field collaboration: Soils, Food and Healthy Communities, Malawi

title: Jane Wangui Mugo: Can climate models tell a farmer where a crop will still work tomorrow?
text:
Jane Wangui Mugo is a Lecturer in Earth and Climate Sciences at the University of Nairobi. Her research sits at the point where climate projections become agricultural decisions. Rather than asking only how temperature or rainfall may change, she asks what those changes mean for a crop in a particular place: whether the crop remains suitable, when it should be planted and how much yield might change. Her University of Nairobi profile describes a programme combining climate modelling, crop simulation, machine learning, remote sensing and GIS.
Mugo trained in meteorology and agrometeorology before completing a PhD in Meteorology at the University of Nairobi. Her doctoral research focused on green gram, a short-duration legume important in Kenya’s arid and semi-arid lands. The work combined observed climate data, downscaled regional climate projections and crop modelling to map how suitability and production could change under future conditions. Her 2021 thesis, Modelling Green Gram Production in Kenya Under the Current and Future Climates, provides a clear intellectual anchor for the career.
The method matters because climate impacts are spatial. A national mean temperature cannot tell a farmer in Kitui whether a crop will mature before rainfall ends. Mugo has used CORDEX regional climate simulations, GIS-based suitability analysis and crop models such as APSIM and AquaCrop to translate climate scenarios into agricultural outcomes. A 2023 Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems paper simulated climate-change effects on green-gram production in Kitui County. Other collaborative work has linked crop simulation with machine learning to predict yield distributions.
Her experience extends beyond Kenya. Mugo has worked as a climate-risks specialist and international consultant with FAO and as a crop modeller with IITA, contributing to climate-data integration, vulnerability mapping and adaptation planning in several countries. In 2023 FAO invited her to present technical approaches for climate-data acquisition in agricultural modelling for adaptation planning in Sudan.
The unresolved problem is uncertainty at decision scale. Climate models become less certain as information is pushed toward a particular farm, season and crop, precisely where users want the most specific answer. Crop models add another layer of assumptions about soils, varieties and management. Mugo’s work therefore confronts a central problem in climate services: how to make projections specific enough to guide action without pretending they are more certain than they are.

Jane Wangui Mugo
Lecturer, University of Nairobi
Field: Agrometeorology and climate modelling
Research focus: Crop simulation, climate risk, GIS and adaptation
Training: PhD Meteorology, University of Nairobi
Selected research: Climate-change simulation of green gram production in Kitui County, 2023

title: Monica Lambon-Quayefio: Does digital credit actually change outcomes for smallholder farmers?
text:
Monica Lambon-Quayefio is an Associate Professor in the University of Ghana’s Department of Economics whose research asks a deceptively simple question: when policy changes what people can do, does it also change what ultimately happens to them? Her work spans social protection, gender, labour markets, education and agriculture, but the common thread is empirical. Interventions are judged against outcomes rather than intentions. The University of Ghana lists her current appointment alongside research affiliations with J-PAL, CEGA, Oxford’s Centre for the Study of African Economies and the Environment for Development initiative.
Lambon-Quayefio completed graduate training in economics at Clark University, receiving an MA in 2010 and a PhD in 2014. She joined the University of Ghana’s economics department and has built an applied research programme using experiments and quasi-experimental methods to examine policies affecting households, women and children. Her work on non-farm employment, education and gender sits beside more recent research on digital technologies in agriculture.
A particularly revealing example is a 2026 Journal of Development Economics paper with Dean Karlan, Utsav Manjeer and Christopher Udry. The study experimentally evaluated a digital lending product for farmers in southern Ghana. Credit increased farm investment, but the researchers found few statistically significant average effects on downstream outcomes such as yield and income. The experiment also encountered an operational complication: some loans arrived in time for agricultural investment while others arrived later, making timing itself part of the explanation. The published study argues cautiously that digital agricultural credit has potential, but that delivery timing deserves much more attention.
That result is important because a null effect can be more informative than a success story. Digital finance is often presented as a way to remove a binding constraint. But if farmers borrow, invest and still do not see strong average gains in production or income, then credit may not be the only constraint. Markets, storage, extension, land, weather risk and the timing of finance may all matter.
The open question is what has to accompany access to credit for welfare effects to appear consistently. Lambon-Quayefio’s broader research suggests the answer will not be one additional input. Policy effects depend on the institutions and inequalities surrounding households. The real test of digital finance is therefore not whether it gets money into farmers’ hands, but whether it changes the outcomes that justified the programme in the first place.

Monica Lambon-Quayefio
Associate Professor, University of Ghana
Field: Applied microeconomics
Research focus: Gender, social protection, labour markets and digital finance
Training: PhD Economics, Clark University, 2014
Selected recent paper: Digital credit for smallholder farmers, Journal of Development Economics (2026)

title: How I got here
text:
Elvis Kwame Ofori standing outdoors in a patterned cardigan.
I studied accounting in Ghana, taught English in China, and now build agricultural and land-use models in Ireland. None of those sentences would have predicted the next one while I was living it. Looking back can make a life seem more carefully planned than it was. Mine was not. There were opportunities I prepared for and decisions I made, but also plans that changed, a visa that arrived too late, people who opened doors, and places that became important long after I first arrived in them. The About page has the short version. This is the longer story.

title: How I got here
text:
Ghana: where it began
I studied Accounting at the University of Professional Studies, Accra. It may seem some distance from the work I do now, but I do not think of it as an abandoned beginning. Accounting taught me to pay attention to numbers and organisations, and to the difference between what something appears to be and what the underlying records actually show. It took me years to see how useful that instinct would become.
After university I did my National Service with Ghana’s National Petroleum Authority. I had been living in Accra, and the posting sent me to Takoradi, one of the first times life moved me somewhere I had not planned to go. It was also my first real taste of responsibility. I worked nights and double shifts and was trusted with supervisory duties. None of it was glamorous, but it was an education of its own. University had taught me concepts; work began to show me what happens when procedures, rules and decisions meet the people expected to carry them out, and how differently an organisation looks depending on where inside it you stand.
I would not have called that an interest in policy implementation at the time. A few years later, however, the same concern returned as research. One of my early papers, published in Resources Policy, examined how to measure safety performance in Ghana’s oil and gas industry. The subject was different from what I work on now, but the underlying question was already familiar: what happens between a formal system and the people who have to make it work?

title: How I got here
section: China: a much bigger change than a degree
text:
China: a much bigger change than a degree
In 2019 I received a full scholarship for an MSc in Management Science and Engineering and moved to Taiyuan, in northern China. I knew China would be different. I was less prepared for how different the north would feel to someone arriving from Ghana, and the cold introduced itself quickly.
The larger change was intellectual. China was where I became deliberate about policy research. Instead of seeing only a result, I started asking what structure had produced it. My interests moved across sustainability, development, environmental policy and energy economics. Energy held my attention because so many of its decisions operate at scale: governments, industries and large companies can change the direction of a whole system, and thinking at that scale taught me to look for the links between institutions, incentives and outcomes.



With people who became part of my life in China.


China became much more than a scholarship or a degree. The people around me became part of the education too.
Part of my life there never appeared on a transcript. I taught English as a second language, including to young children, and I loved the moment when confusion turned into confidence and something difficult suddenly made sense. Years later I realised that teaching had sharpened a skill research needs too: understanding something yourself is one thing, and explaining it clearly to someone else is another. The same instinct showed up when colleagues needed help with data. I liked sitting down with someone and working through not only which command to run, but what the numbers were saying and whether the interpretation held up. I still think of data analysis almost as a conversation. You learn how to talk to data, and you also have to learn when to stop talking long enough to let the data answer back.



Teaching English in China, with two of my younger students.


I later began doctoral study in China as well. That path would change, but China had already changed me.

title: How I got here
text:
What moving teaches you
I left Ghana in 2019. I could not have known then that I would not go home again until 2024. Living abroad brought opportunities that changed my life, and it also taught me that mobility is not experienced equally. For some people international travel is mostly a ticket, a passport and a timetable. For others it means visa applications, appointments, waiting and the real possibility that an opportunity will move faster than the paperwork.
I learned this clearly with Germany. I was due to join colleagues at a capacity-building training there. They did not face the same visa requirement; I did. By the time my visa arrived, the training was over. I eventually travelled to Germany, but as a personal trip rather than for the programme that had made the journey necessary. It was hardly a tragedy, but it stayed with me because it showed something that talk of international mobility tends to hide: an opportunity can be equally available on paper and still be much easier for one person to reach than another.



By the river in Berlin, on the later trip.

title: How I got here
text:
Ireland: beginning again
Eventually I left the doctoral path I had begun in China and moved to the University of Galway for a different PhD. Before the research groups, conferences and models became part of the story, Ireland was simply somewhere new, and a new country means learning small things all over again: routes, weather, shops, ways of speaking, and the rules nobody explains because everyone else already knows them.



My first day in Ireland.


Then the research moved sideways in a way I had not expected. Much of my earlier work was in energy economics, where the important actors were governments, industries and large institutions. Agriculture and land use brought the problem much closer to individual decisions. A government can set a climate target, a model can describe a pathway, and a sector can be told that its emissions must fall. But eventually somebody owns or works the land. Somebody has animals to feed, bills to pay, machinery already bought, a family involved in the farm, or a perfectly good reason for continuing to do something that looks inefficient from far away. That pulled my attention towards farmers, land-use decisions, behavioural responses and the way costs are distributed across people and places. Later, while continuing the PhD, I joined the wider FORESIGHT and FUSION research environment at Galway as a Research Assistant.






With colleagues from the FORESIGHT and FUSION research environment at the University of Galway.







At the Agriculture & Land Use in Ireland conference.





Research eventually gave me a community as well as a subject.
The subject had changed a great deal since accounting and my energy work, but some of the underlying questions had changed less than I first thought. By Ireland, I could state them more plainly: Who makes the decision, and with what information? Which constraints disappear when you look from too far away? Who benefits, and who pays? A national model may say that livestock numbers should fall, that land should change use or that a technology should be adopted. A farmer still has to decide what to do on Monday morning. The distance between the aggregate pathway and that decision has become the part of the work I care about most.
Read more about my research →
Work helps a place become home, but work alone does not make a life. Church, shared meals, friendships and ordinary routines are what turned Ireland from somewhere I had moved for a PhD into somewhere that holds pieces of my life. There have been classmates who became friends, colleagues who patiently explained things I probably should have known, supervisors who trusted me, and people who helped when I was new. A CV is good at recording institutions and much worse at recording people. It records the year you arrived; it does not record who helped make the place feel less strange.



After church in Galway, waiting for lunch with members of the church community.

title: How I got here
text:
Beyond the desk
Research has also given me reasons to travel. One trip took me to Washington, D.C., for the World Bank LAND Conference. The programme was the formal reason for going, but a conference is rarely only its programme. There are conversations over coffee, people you did not expect to meet, and a city you had previously known mostly through books and news. In Washington I met other Ghanaians at the conference, a small reminder that home can turn up in unexpected places.



With other Ghanaian participants at the World Bank LAND Conference in Washington, D.C.

title: How I got here
text:
Going home
For all the places that became part of my life after 2019, Ghana never stopped being home. I returned for the first time in 2024, five years after leaving, and went back again in 2025. Five years is long enough for absence to become normal. You learn to celebrate some things through a screen, hear family news over the phone and accept that ordinary moments are happening without you. Going home changed the scale of those years.



With my parents in Ghana, on a return visit.


What mattered was not sightseeing but family: sitting together, talking without watching the time, eating together, being physically present again. Living abroad has given me opportunities I am deeply grateful for, but opportunity and family are not interchangeable. A career can cross borders surprisingly well. Relationships still depend on presence.
