title: Jacqueline Naalamle Amissah: Can plants that have rarely been farmed become useful crops before they disappear?
text:
Jacqueline Naalamle Amissah is an Associate Professor in the University of Ghana’s Department of Crop Science whose work focuses on a category of plants agriculture often overlooks: species that are useful, culturally important or biologically interesting but have never been domesticated on the scale of major crops. Her research spans propagation, horticulture and plant tissue culture, with particular attention to species that are difficult to multiply or vulnerable in the wild. The University of Ghana’s research system records research activity from 2008 onward across horticulture, indigenous crops and sustainable production.
Amissah trained in agriculture in Ghana before moving to Cornell University for graduate study in horticulture, completing an MSc and then a PhD. She returned to the University of Ghana and developed a programme around propagation biology and domestication. That work has included shea, miracle fruit and Cryptolepis sanguinolenta, a medicinal plant used in malaria treatment. The scientific problem is practical: many wild or semi-domesticated species do not reproduce easily under cultivation, so conservation and commercialisation both depend on learning how to propagate them reliably.
One important strand of her work has therefore been tissue culture and vegetative propagation. In the case of Cryptolepis sanguinolenta, research supported through an international collaboration developed protocols aimed at moving the species from pressure on wild populations toward cultivation. More recent work has expanded into indigenous fruits and vegetables, seed physiology, tomato production and the profitability of underused crops across West Africa. A 2026 University of Ghana record includes research on spatial variation in profitability among indigenous fruit and vegetable farmers and on consumer-led product development for indigenous foods.
That movement from laboratory to market is central to the career. A successful tissue-culture protocol solves only the first stage of domestication. Farmers still need planting material, extension support, markets and reasons to take on an unfamiliar crop. Consumers must also recognise value in the product. Amissah’s research increasingly sits across those stages, from multiplication of plants to the food-system conditions that determine whether an underused species becomes economically viable.
The unresolved question is scale. Many indigenous and medicinal plants have desirable traits, but agriculture is built around systems designed for a relatively small number of well-established crops. Moving a species from the wild into a farmer’s field requires more than proving that it can be propagated. It requires a chain of biological, agronomic and market solutions. Amissah’s work asks whether that chain can be built quickly enough to conserve useful plants while also creating new options for farmers and food systems.

Jacqueline Naalamle Amissah
Associate Professor, University of Ghana
Field: Horticulture and plant tissue culture
Research focus: Plant domestication, propagation and underutilised species
Training: Graduate horticulture training at Cornell University
Current themes: Indigenous fruits and vegetables, propagation and sustainable horticulture

title: Eve Daly: Can we see enough of the soil to manage water and carbon better?
text:
Eve Daly is a geophysicist and lecturer in Earth and Ocean Sciences at the University of Galway. Her work focuses on the critical zone, the permeable layer from vegetation through soil to groundwater where rock, water and life interact. Her Galway profile describes a research programme built around imaging this hidden layer for applications in water resources, agriculture and climate accounting.
Daly trained first in physics and later completed a PhD in geophysics. In 2019 she established the HY-RES research group, bringing together hydrogeophysics and remote sensing. The recurring problem is measurement. Soil moisture, peat depth, compaction and subsurface water are important for farm management and carbon inventories, but they are difficult to observe continuously and at useful spatial scales.
Her group combines field geophysics, satellite observations, airborne radiometric data and machine-learning methods. Recent work has used Ireland’s Tellus survey to map peat beneath grassland and forest cover, investigated soil compaction associated with cattle grazing and developed soil-moisture products for drainage and crop management. In 2026, Daly and collaborators published work in SOIL on the effects of rewetting agricultural fen peat through drain blocking.
The science is closely tied to national accounting. Projects with Teagasc, Trinity College Dublin and Munster Technological University are developing tools for greenhouse-gas reporting and peatland management. Daly also serves on the Royal Irish Academy’s Geosciences Committee and a Met Éireann–Teagasc working group on agricultural meteorology.
The unresolved challenge is scale. Measurements that work well in one field do not automatically translate into national maps, while national remote-sensing products can miss local hydrology. Daly’s work sits in that gap, asking how multiple sensing systems can be combined closely enough to inform both farm decisions and national climate reporting.

Eve Daly
Lecturer, University of Galway
Field: Geophysics and Earth observation
Research focus: Critical-zone imaging, soil moisture and peat
Research group: HY-RES, established 2019
Selected recent paper: Agricultural fen peat rewetting, SOIL (2026)

title: Jane Ambuko: How do you stop food from being lost after it has already been grown?
text:
Jane Ambuko is a horticultural scientist at the University of Nairobi whose work begins after a crop has been harvested. The problem is deceptively simple. Farmers can produce food successfully and still lose a substantial part of its value before it is eaten because of bruising, heat, poor storage, weak cold chains, transport delays and market conditions. Ambuko has built her research around reducing those losses without assuming that smallholder farmers can simply purchase expensive infrastructure. The University of Nairobi Postharvest Project describes her work as adaptive research that validates and scales postharvest technologies for smallholder settings.
Ambuko trained in agriculture and horticulture at the University of Nairobi before completing a PhD in Agricultural Sciences, with a horticulture and postharvest focus, at the University of Tsukuba in Japan. Her university career combines teaching, student supervision, research and outreach. Over time, the research moved increasingly toward the practical systems connecting farms to consumers: how fruit and vegetables are cooled, handled, stored, processed and marketed, and which technologies are affordable enough to survive outside a controlled research environment.
That laboratory-to-field movement became the organising theme of her 2024 professorial inaugural lecture, From the Lab to the Land: Solutions for Food Loss & Waste Reduction for the People and the Planet. The University of Nairobi presented the lecture as the culmination of research on food-loss reduction and practical application. Her team has worked on low-cost cooling and storage, solar drying, improved handling and farmer training, linking technical interventions with the people expected to use them.
Ambuko’s programme is also institutional. The university’s postharvest platform combines research with training and community outreach, so students, farmers and other actors in the food chain become part of how technologies are tested. This matters because a technically effective intervention can fail if it requires electricity that is unreliable, maintenance skills that are unavailable or capital that farmers cannot access.
The unresolved question is therefore not whether postharvest losses can be reduced. Many technologies already demonstrate that they can. The harder problem is adoption at scale. A solution has to preserve food, fit local market practices, repay its cost and remain usable after a research project ends. Ambuko’s career has increasingly been about that final distance between a successful experiment and food that actually reaches a consumer.

Jane Ambuko
Professor of Horticulture, University of Nairobi
Field: Horticulture and postharvest science
Research focus: Food loss and waste, postharvest technologies and smallholder systems
Training: University of Nairobi; PhD, University of Tsukuba
Selected career marker: 50th University of Nairobi professorial inaugural lecture, 2024

title: Sinéad Waters: Can the rumen be changed enough to cut methane without weakening livestock production?
text:
Sinéad Waters is a lecturer and principal investigator at the University of Galway whose research focuses on the microbial communities living inside ruminant animals. The practical problem is methane. Cattle and other ruminants depend on microorganisms in the rumen to break down feed that the animal itself cannot digest efficiently. Methane is produced within that microbial ecosystem, which means reducing emissions is not simply a matter of removing an unwanted by-product. The intervention has to change a functioning biological system without damaging the processes that sustain animal health and productivity. Galway describes that host–microbiome interaction as the core of her current programme.
Waters spent almost two decades at Teagasc, from 2005 until early 2024, before joining the University of Galway. Across that period she built a research programme using animal science, molecular biology, genomics, transcriptomics, microbiology and bioinformatics. She also served as co-chair of the Livestock Research Group of the Global Research Alliance for Agricultural Greenhouse Gases from 2018 to 2023 and has represented Ireland in European expert work on agricultural methane.
Her laboratory question is increasingly connected to technologies being considered for farms. Waters studies feed additives, breeding strategies and microbial responses that might reduce enteric methane. Recent papers have examined brown-seaweed hydrolysates and temperate seaweeds for their effects on rumen fermentation and methane production. These studies are part of a larger shift in methane research from measuring the problem toward identifying interventions that can survive the transition from controlled experiments to pasture-based livestock systems.
Teaching gives another view of how the field is changing. Galway lists Waters as module owner for Food and Industry Microbiology and Microbiomes Underpinning Agriculture, alongside teaching on agricultural greenhouse-gas emissions, rumen microbiology, methane mitigation and livestock genomics. She also supervises student research projects and contributes to the MSc in Agriculture, Sustainability and Technology.
The difficult question is biological robustness. An additive that suppresses methane in vitro may behave differently in an animal, under grazing conditions or over long periods. Microbial communities can adapt, responses can vary between animals and an intervention that alters fermentation may affect productivity or health. Waters’ work therefore sits at the point where national methane targets meet a living ecosystem. Cutting methane is possible in principle. The harder task is finding interventions that remain effective, safe and economically usable once they leave the laboratory.

Sinéad Waters
Lecturer, University of Galway
Field: Rumen microbiology and animal science
Research focus: Methane mitigation, microbiomes and host–animal interactions
Career: Teagasc, 2005–2024; University of Galway, from 2024
Teaching: Microbiomes, agricultural greenhouse gases, rumen biology and livestock genomics

title: Cecilia Onyango: How do indigenous vegetables move from neglected crops into mainstream food systems?
text:
Cecilia Moraa Onyango is an Associate Professor in the University of Nairobi’s Department of Plant Science and Crop Protection. Her research has repeatedly returned to crops that sit between agriculture, nutrition and culture, especially African indigenous vegetables. These crops are often well adapted to local environments and valued in household diets, yet they can remain marginal in formal breeding, supply chains and agricultural policy. The University of Nairobi lists her specialisation as agronomy and horticulture.
Onyango joined the university as an assistant lecturer in 2001 and completed a PhD in Horticulture at Wageningen University in 2010, after earlier agriculture and horticulture degrees at Nairobi. An early strand of her work examined how traditional leafy vegetables were handled and sold in Nairobi. A 2007 study surveyed supermarkets and independent greengrocers, showing that crops such as amaranth, African nightshade and spider plant were already circulating through urban markets but often with limited formal packaging and postharvest support.
The research later widened from handling to production, use and conservation. Onyango and collaborators documented spider plant as an underutilised leafy vegetable with ecological, cultural and nutritional value, and studied African nightshade production and indigenous knowledge across Kenyan communities. These are not simply exercises in cataloguing neglected crops. They ask what makes a species move from household gardens and local markets into more reliable production systems without losing the diversity and knowledge that made it useful in the first place.
More recently, Onyango has also become involved in the institutional problem of connecting research to policy. In 2025 she was named leader of a Kenyan Science Translation Hub supported through the AgriFoSe2030 programme, designed to help early-career researchers communicate evidence from food and agricultural science into policy processes. That role extends the same translation problem from crops to knowledge itself.
The unresolved question is scale without simplification. Indigenous vegetables can contribute to nutrition, resilience and crop diversity, but mainstreaming them may favour a small number of standardised varieties and supply chains. The task is therefore not just to make neglected crops more visible. It is to build production, markets and policy around them in ways that preserve the diversity and local knowledge that made them valuable.

Cecilia Moraa Onyango
Associate Professor, University of Nairobi
Field: Agronomy and horticulture
Research focus: Indigenous vegetables, crop production and food-system research
Training: PhD Horticulture, Wageningen University, 2010
Early publication anchor: Postharvest handling of traditional leafy vegetables in Nairobi, 2007

title: Pearl Abu: Can maize be bred for yield, nutrition and stress tolerance at the same time?
text:
Pearl Abu is a plant breeder at the West Africa Centre for Crop Improvement at the University of Ghana, where her work focuses on maize for difficult growing conditions in sub-Saharan Africa. The breeding problem is not one-dimensional. Farmers need varieties that yield reliably under low soil nitrogen, drought and parasitic weeds such as Striga hermonthica. Consumers also benefit when grain contains more protein, provitamin A or zinc. Abu’s research asks whether those traits can be combined rather than traded against one another.
She trained in agronomy and plant breeding before completing a PhD in Plant Breeding through WACCI in 2019. Her research record reaches back to work on maize genotype stability under different nitrogen conditions and developed through studies of extra-early quality-protein maize, low-nitrogen tolerance and resistance to Striga. Those are important traits in environments where farmers cannot always compensate for poor soils with large fertiliser applications.
Her current programme goes beyond conventional selection. Abu is working with doubled-haploid technology, which can accelerate the production of genetically uniform breeding lines and shorten the time needed to develop new varieties. She has also explored arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi as biological partners that may improve nutrient uptake while reducing dependence on chemical fertiliser. In 2025, UNESCO recognised her as one of the first laureates of the UNESCO-Equatorial Guinea fellowship for young women scientists in Africa, citing her work on protein- and provitamin-A enriched, stress-tolerant maize and Ghana’s first doubled-haploid maize breeding platform.
The science is therefore about stacking advantages. A maize line that performs well under low nitrogen may not automatically have strong nutritional quality. A high-yielding variety may be susceptible to Striga. A technically superior line may also take years to move through testing, seed multiplication and farmer adoption. Breeding is an exercise in balancing these constraints over successive generations.
That last step remains the complication. A variety has no impact until seed reaches farmers and farmers decide it is worth planting. Traits that breeders value must survive contact with seed systems, farmer preferences, local markets and highly variable field conditions. Abu’s work sits at the productive tension between genetic improvement and adoption. The question is not only whether maize can be improved on several fronts at once, but whether the resulting varieties can move quickly enough from breeding programme to farm to matter.

Pearl Abu
Senior Lecturer, West Africa Centre for Crop Improvement
Field: Plant breeding and genetics
Research focus: Climate-resilient maize, biofortification and doubled haploids
Training: PhD Plant Breeding, University of Ghana, 2019
Recognition: UNESCO-Equatorial Guinea Fellowship for Young Women Scientists in Africa, 2025

title: Britta Rennkamp: Can a rapid energy transition also reduce structural inequality?
text:
Britta Rennkamp is a Senior Researcher at the University of Cape Town’s African Climate and Development Initiative and co-director of the ARUA Centre of Excellence in Climate and Development. Her work sits at the intersection of climate policy, energy policy, inequality and political economy. The question is not simply how a country replaces high-carbon technologies. It is how that transition unfolds in societies where unemployment, poverty and unequal access to power are already structural features. ACDI describes her current programme as examining the two-way relationship between climate policy and social inequality across sub-Saharan Africa.
Rennkamp trained in science and technology policy at the University of Twente after earlier interdisciplinary study of Latin America at the University of Cologne. Before joining UCT, she worked with German development institutions in Brazil and Germany. That background gave her a comparative view of how technology, industrial policy and development institutions shape transitions in very different political settings.
Her research has examined renewable energy, coal, nuclear power, carbon taxation and green industrial policy. One influential Climate Policy paper analysed power, coalitions and institutional change in South African climate policy using parliamentary records, media, public comments and interviews. It found that policy change becomes especially fragile when powerful actors face direct losses, and that poverty language can sometimes be used strategically by actors protecting established interests. The paper makes transition politics concrete by showing how policies move through competing coalitions rather than through technical optimisation alone.
That emphasis carries into her current work on just energy transitions. Rennkamp has managed research and consulting projects and multi-stakeholder engagements across Africa, Europe and Latin America. She also contributes to international assessments, including the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report and work on clean-energy innovation in emerging and developing economies.
The unresolved tension is that “just transition” can serve opposite political purposes. It can create a framework for sharing costs, protecting workers and building legitimacy for faster climate action. It can also become a language for delaying change when powerful interests attach their losses to broader claims about social protection. Rennkamp’s work asks which coalitions are able to turn climate policy into durable institutional change. The deeper question is whether transition politics can redistribute power at the same time as it redistributes energy.

Britta Rennkamp
Senior Researcher, African Climate and Development Initiative
Field: Climate policy and science, technology and innovation policy
Research focus: Just energy transitions, inequality, governance and political economy
Selected role: Co-director, ARUA Centre of Excellence in Climate and Development
Selected publication: Power, coalitions and institutional change in South African climate policy, Climate Policy (2019)

title: Agnes Mwang’ombe: How do you build crop protection science that lasts beyond one disease outbreak?
text:
Agnes Wakesho Mwang’ombe is a Professor of Plant Pathology at the University of Nairobi. Her career belongs to an earlier generation of African plant scientists who were not only expected to investigate crop diseases but also to build the university programmes, laboratories and training systems that would produce the next generation of specialists. The University of Nairobi’s history of plant pathology places her within the development of postgraduate plant-pathology training at the institution.
Mwang’ombe studied agriculture and plant pathology at Nairobi before receiving a Commonwealth Scholarship for doctoral training at Imperial College in London in the 1980s. She returned to the University of Nairobi and joined the department in 1988. Her academic career subsequently combined research in crop protection with administration and postgraduate education, including service as Dean of Agriculture and as principal of the former College of Agriculture and Veterinary Sciences.
Plant pathology is necessarily applied science. Disease emerges through interactions among pathogens, susceptible crops, environments and farming practices. Mwang’ombe’s research has ranged across crop diseases and food-security questions, while her later work has also connected agricultural production to nutrition, poverty alleviation and environmental sustainability. The university continues to identify her as a programme leader in doctoral plant pathology, making training itself part of the scientific legacy.
That institutional contribution matters because plant disease control cannot be reduced to a single successful treatment. New pathogens arrive, climates change, varieties lose resistance and farmers alter crops and management. A durable crop-protection system therefore depends on diagnostic capacity and trained scientists as much as on a particular fungicide or resistant variety. Mwang’ombe’s career spans both sides of that problem: producing agricultural knowledge and building the institutions capable of renewing it.
The unresolved question is how crop-protection science keeps pace with increasingly connected agricultural systems. Pathogens move across borders, climate change alters disease pressure and farmers need solutions that are biologically effective but economically realistic. The answer cannot be one permanent technology. It requires institutions able to detect, study and respond repeatedly. That may be the most consequential part of a career that has lasted across several generations of Kenyan agricultural science.

Agnes W. Mwang’ombe
Professor of Plant Pathology, University of Nairobi
Field: Plant pathology
Research focus: Crop disease, food security and agricultural training
Training: MSc, University of Nairobi; PhD/DIC, Imperial College London
University career: Joined the Department of Plant Science and Crop Protection in 1988

title: Gina Ziervogel: Who bears the trade-offs when cities adapt to climate change?
text:
Gina Ziervogel is Professor at the University of Cape Town and Director of the African Climate and Development Initiative. Her work is concerned with adaptation, but not in the narrow sense of finding a technical response to a climate hazard. She studies how vulnerability is produced by governance, inequality and development decisions, and how those conditions shape who benefits when governments respond to drought, flooding or heat. UCT describes her research as spanning neighbourhoods, NGOs, cities, provinces and national institutions across Southern Africa.
Ziervogel trained as a geographer, completing her doctorate at the University of Oxford in 2002 after earlier study in South Africa. Over roughly twenty-five years she has worked on climate vulnerability and adaptation in settings where environmental risk is inseparable from poverty, infrastructure and political power. Her methodological preference is engaged and transdisciplinary research, bringing communities, civil society, government and academics into the same process rather than treating adaptation as a purely expert exercise.
Cape Town’s drought provides one of the clearest examples. The city’s water crisis became an international story about reservoirs and “Day Zero”, but Ziervogel’s work has emphasised that drought impacts were distributed through existing inequalities in housing, water access and municipal capacity. Similar questions appear in her research on flooding and urban adaptation. A protective intervention can reduce risk in one place while shifting costs elsewhere, and the people most exposed to climate hazards often have the least influence over the decisions made on their behalf.
Ziervogel was a lead author of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report chapter on Cities, Settlements and Key Infrastructure. She has also worked through public-facing forms including a book on Cape Town’s drought, documentary collaboration and climate-justice material for schools. In August 2026, her UCT inaugural lecture returned explicitly to the question of trade-offs in climate adaptation.
That is the unresolved problem. Adaptation is often presented as an obvious good, but almost every intervention allocates money, land, protection, inconvenience and risk. Those choices are political even when expressed through engineering or planning language. Ziervogel’s work asks whether participatory approaches can do more than reveal disagreement. The harder test is whether they can redistribute decision-making power enough to produce adaptation that is not only effective, but also more just.

Gina Ziervogel
Professor and Director, African Climate and Development Initiative
Field: Climate adaptation and governance
Research focus: Vulnerability, urban adaptation, inequality and participatory research
Training: PhD Geography, University of Oxford, 2002
Selected role: Lead author, IPCC AR6 chapter on Cities, Settlements and Key Infrastructure

title: Katye Altieri: What can the remote Southern Ocean tell us about a climate before industrial pollution?
text:
Katye Altieri is an Associate Professor of Oceanography at the University of Cape Town whose research follows material moving between ocean and atmosphere. She studies marine aerosols, atmospheric chemistry, biogeochemistry and air–sea interactions, with a particular interest in the Southern Ocean. UCT lists her research across atmospheric observations and modelling, marine biogeochemistry, climate change and air pollution. The scientific question is difficult because aerosols remain one of the less certain parts of the climate system, especially over remote oceans where observations are scarce.
Altieri trained in chemistry before completing a PhD in Oceanography at Rutgers University. She then held postdoctoral appointments supported by the NOAA Climate and Global Change programme and at Princeton and Brown. Her career also includes training in public policy, an unusual combination that reflects the distance her work travels between basic atmospheric chemistry and questions with consequences for climate modelling and environmental decision-making.
Much of her current research uses the Southern Ocean as a natural laboratory. Winter cruises on the SA Agulhas II allow her group to sample air and seawater far from dense population centres. One aim is to understand the sources and chemical composition of marine aerosols, including nitrogen-containing particles. These observations can help researchers test how well the remote marine atmosphere approximates conditions before large-scale industrial emissions altered atmospheric chemistry. Recent work has used nitrogen stable isotopes to distinguish ammonia sources and trace the formation of ammonium aerosol in the marine boundary layer.
The field setting is part of the science. The Southern Ocean is remote, stormy and difficult to sample, so every observation comes from an environment in which logistics constrain the data. At the same time, those conditions make the region scientifically valuable. In 2025, Altieri received the Oppenheimer Memorial Trust New Frontiers Research Award for work linking atmospheric nitrogen, marine aerosols and climate processes.
The unresolved question is whether the Southern Ocean can continue to serve as a useful window onto a preindustrial atmosphere while the ocean itself is changing. Human influence reaches even remote environments through long-range pollution, greenhouse warming and changing ocean circulation. The better scientists become at detecting those signals, the harder it becomes to assume that any place is untouched. Altieri’s work therefore uses remoteness not as proof of purity, but as a hypothesis that has to be tested repeatedly.

Katye Altieri
Associate Professor, University of Cape Town
Field: Oceanography and atmospheric chemistry
Research focus: Marine aerosols, atmosphere–ocean interactions and climate
Field platform: Southern Ocean research cruises on the SA Agulhas II
Recognition: Oppenheimer Memorial Trust New Frontiers Research Award, 2025

title: Hannah Ritchie: Can better data change how people think about environmental progress?
text:
Hannah Ritchie is a Senior Researcher, Deputy Editor and Science Outreach Lead at Our World in Data and an Oxford Martin Fellow. Her work asks how environmental and development debates change when long-run evidence replaces impressions, headlines and isolated statistics. The Oxford Martin School describes her research across food supply, agriculture, energy, climate, biodiversity and global health.
Ritchie trained in environmental geoscience and carbon management before completing a PhD in geosciences at the University of Edinburgh. She also taught sustainability there. Her research career gradually moved toward building and interpreting global datasets that allow readers to compare countries, technologies and trends across long periods.
Food systems have been a major theme. Ritchie has published on whether global agriculture can meet nutritional needs while reducing environmental pressure, how much land food production requires and the consequences of alternative diets and farming systems. At Our World in Data, the scientific task is inseparable from communication. The charts and datasets are designed to make claims inspectable rather than merely persuasive.
That approach can produce conclusions that cut against both pessimistic and complacent narratives. Some indicators improve while others deteriorate. Agricultural land use can peak even as biodiversity pressures remain severe. Clean technologies can expand rapidly while total emissions remain too high. Ritchie’s work is strongest when it holds those facts together rather than forcing them into one story of progress or collapse.
The unresolved question is whether evidence changes public reasoning. Better data can correct false beliefs, but political identity, values and unequal attention still shape what people accept. The challenge is therefore not only to measure environmental change accurately. It is to communicate it in a way that preserves uncertainty, scale and context without losing the reader.

Hannah Ritchie
Senior Researcher and Deputy Editor, Our World in Data
Field: Sustainability data science
Research focus: Food, energy, climate, biodiversity and development
Training: PhD GeoSciences, University of Edinburgh
Oxford role: Oxford Martin Fellow

title: Marianna Siegmund-Schultze: How do farming systems change without losing the people inside them?
text:
Marianna Siegmund-Schultze leads the Land Use and Food Security team in Wageningen Plant Research. Her work treats farms not as isolated production units but as social-ecological systems shaped by people, animals, soils, markets and institutions. Wageningen describes her programme as using integrative and systemic approaches to understand farming and agri-food transitions.
Her research trajectory has moved across very different agricultural settings. Her graduation work examined urban livestock keeping in Burkina Faso. Her PhD focused on smallholder cattle systems in the eastern Amazon, and she later completed a habilitation in livestock husbandry systems at the University of Hohenheim. Those experiences established the comparative perspective that still characterises her work.
At Wageningen she combines team leadership with research on agroecology, biodiversity, climate and soil, social transitions and multi-stakeholder governance. Her projects span the Netherlands and international settings in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Rather than asking only which technology performs best, the work asks how interventions fit into livelihood strategies, institutions and ecological limits.
That perspective is particularly important in debates about circular and regenerative agriculture. A measure that looks efficient at farm scale may shift burdens to another region, increase labour demands or conflict with household priorities. Systems analysis is useful precisely because it forces those interactions into view.
The unresolved question is how much complexity decision-making can absorb. Integrated approaches reveal more of reality, but policy still needs choices that can be implemented. Siegmund-Schultze’s work sits in the difficult space between a model rich enough to represent farming systems and a recommendation simple enough for institutions and farmers to act on.

Marianna Siegmund-Schultze
Team Lead, Land Use and Food Security, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Agricultural systems and land use
Research focus: Agroecology, governance and farming-system transitions
Early settings: Burkina Faso and eastern Amazonia
Current team: Land Use and Food Security

title: Hester Biemans: How much water can agriculture use in a warming world?
text:
Hester Biemans is a Special Professor in Earth Systems and Global Change and a researcher in Water and Food at Wageningen University & Research. Her work sits at one of the most consequential resource constraints in agriculture: water. Wageningen’s research portal identifies climate change, hydrology and food security as the core of her programme.
Biemans studies how river flow, irrigation demand, reservoirs and crop production interact across large regions. Her research often uses global and regional hydrological models to connect climate scenarios to agricultural water availability. That scale matters because water stress in one basin may affect food production, trade and prices far beyond the farms using the water.
A recurring concern is irrigation. Irrigation can protect yields from rainfall variability, but it also depends on rivers, groundwater and infrastructure that may themselves become less reliable under climate change. Biemans has worked extensively on South Asia, where glacier-fed rivers, monsoon systems and intensive irrigation create a particularly complex water-food relationship.
Her work brings together physical hydrology and food-system consequences. Instead of treating water scarcity only as an environmental indicator, she asks what changing supply means for crop calendars, irrigation reliability and the capacity of farming systems to meet demand. That makes adaptation a question of both water engineering and agricultural structure.
The unresolved issue is allocation. Models can estimate how much water exists and how demand might change, but deciding who receives scarce water is political and institutional. Agriculture competes with cities, ecosystems, industry and energy systems. Biemans’ science can make the physical constraint clearer. It cannot by itself settle how societies should distribute that constraint.

Hester Biemans
Special Professor and Researcher, Wageningen University & Research
Field: Hydrology and food security
Research focus: Water resources, irrigation and climate change
Primary setting: Global and regional water-food systems
Core question: Agricultural water availability under climate change

title: Freda Elikplim Asem: Why can productive smallholders still struggle to capture value from food markets?
text:
Freda Elikplim Asem is an Associate Professor in the University of Ghana’s Department of Agricultural Economics and Agribusiness and the West Africa Regional Hub Coordinator for the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Horticulture. Her work begins from a problem that agricultural policy often treats too narrowly. A farmer can improve production and still receive a poor return if the market around that farm is weak, contracts are absent, information is uneven or buyers hold more bargaining power. The University of Ghana describes her research as centred on agribusiness, agricultural marketing, agrifood systems and value-chain analysis, with a particular concern for the livelihoods of smallholder farmers.
Asem trained first in agricultural economics at the University of Ghana, then completed an MSc in Agricultural and Resource Economics at the University of Alberta and a PhD in Development Studies at the University of Ghana. Before joining the present phase of her academic career, she worked at the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research and built more than two decades of experience across agricultural research and development. That mixed background helps explain why her work moves easily between farm-level productivity and the institutions connecting farmers to processors, traders and consumers.
Her research on horticultural value chains has repeatedly shown that technical efficiency is only one part of the problem. Smallholders may produce well and still lose value through weak market information, limited formal contracting and unequal relationships with intermediaries. More recent work widens the lens. In 2026, Asem co-authored research on credit access, rice productivity and farmer welfare in Ghana, crop diversification spillovers and purchasing of indigenous fruits and vegetables across West Africa. Her current projects also link value-chain analysis to climate variability and sustainable crop and fish farming.
That breadth matters because agrifood systems are not chains in the simple sense. Decisions at one point alter incentives elsewhere. A crop that is profitable in one district may be unattractive in another because transport costs differ. Farmers may respond to credit but still face poor prices. Consumers may value indigenous foods but lack reliable access. Asem’s work connects these pieces rather than treating farm output as the final outcome.
The unresolved question is therefore institutional. If smallholders already know how to produce, what has to change around them for more of the value to remain with the people doing the farming? Better information, stronger producer organisations, improved finance and more reliable contracts are all possible answers, but each changes bargaining power differently. Asem’s work keeps the focus on that distributional question: not only whether an agrifood system produces more, but who benefits when it does.

Freda Elikplim Asem
Associate Professor, University of Ghana
Field: Agricultural economics and agribusiness
Research focus: Agrifood value chains, markets and smallholder welfare
Experience: More than 20 years in the agricultural sector
Recent work: Credit, crop diversification and indigenous food markets, 2026

title: Sarah Sparrow: Can citizen computing help us understand extreme weather?
text:
Sarah Sparrow is based at Oxford’s e-Research Centre, where she coordinates climateprediction.net and serves as Deputy Course Director for the MSc in Energy Systems. Her research uses very large ensembles of climate simulations to ask whether and how climate change alters extreme events. Oxford Engineering Science describes her work as coupling climate-model output to impact models across sectors.
Sparrow trained first in chemistry and molecular physics at the University of Nottingham before completing a DPhil in Atmospheric Physics at Oxford. A period in IT consultancy added software-development experience that later became useful in climate computing. She returned to academia to work on atmospheric variability, large model ensembles and the infrastructure required to run them.
The distinctive platform is climateprediction.net, one of the longest-running citizen-science climate projects. Instead of relying only on institutional supercomputers, the project distributes model experiments across thousands of volunteered computers. That allows researchers to generate very large ensembles, which are especially useful for rare events where a small sample of model runs cannot adequately estimate probability.
Sparrow has used these ensembles to study attribution and impacts in areas including flooding, health, energy and finance. The work is interdisciplinary by necessity. A climate simulation becomes policy-relevant only when it connects to an impact model that can say something about disease risk, power-system reliability or another real-world consequence.
The unresolved problem is interpretation. More model runs can narrow sampling uncertainty, but they do not remove uncertainty in model structure, observations or future emissions. Citizen computing can make the experiment larger. The scientific challenge is deciding what that extra scale actually allows us to say about changing risk.

Sarah Sparrow
Professor / CPDN Programme Coordinator, University of Oxford
Field: Climate modelling and attribution
Research focus: Extreme weather, large ensembles and citizen science
Training: DPhil Atmospheric Physics, Oxford
Platform: climateprediction.net

title: Jessica Thorn: Can nature-based adaptation work in the places facing the fastest change?
text:
Jessica Thorn is Assistant Professor in Global Food Security and Environmental Change at Imperial College London and a researcher affiliated with the University of Namibia. Born and raised in Namibia, she works on landscapes where climate change, biodiversity, food security and rapid urbanisation meet. Her central question is not simply whether nature can reduce climate risk. It is whether nature-based solutions can work under the social, ecological and infrastructure pressures found in rapidly changing African cities and rural landscapes. Imperial lists her in the Centre for Environmental Policy.
Thorn’s academic background crosses climate adaptation, ecology and human geography. That combination matters because an intervention such as restoring a wetland or creating urban green infrastructure has both ecological mechanisms and social consequences. Her work uses participatory methods, spatial and ecological evidence, scenario development and collaboration with communities and decision-makers rather than treating adaptation as a purely technical design problem.
She leads the African Nature Futures Lab and the FLOURISH programme, which examines green infrastructure and hydrometeorological risk in informal and peri-urban settlements in Namibia, Madagascar and Sierra Leone. The lab describes the programme as testing how future landscape configurations can improve resilience and ecosystem health. The geography is important. These are places where infrastructure deficits, land-use change and climate hazards interact, making simple comparisons with well-serviced cities misleading.
Her work also reaches into scientific assessment and training. Thorn has contributed to Africa-focused climate assessments and has built a programme around developing research capacity and future scenarios with African collaborators. In 2026 she was recognised as an inaugural African Planet Prize winner for research contributing to planetary-boundary science and environmental resilience.
The complication is that “nature-based solution” can become a label attached to very different projects. Greening a landscape does not guarantee that flood risk falls, biodiversity improves or vulnerable residents benefit. Land can become more valuable and more contested after environmental improvements. Thorn’s work therefore asks for evidence on both ecological effectiveness and distribution. The unresolved question is how to design nature-based adaptation so that the people facing the greatest climate risk also have meaningful power over the landscapes being transformed.

Jessica Thorn
Assistant Professor, Imperial College London; affiliated researcher, University of Namibia
Field: Global food security and environmental change
Research focus: Nature-based solutions, adaptation and African landscape futures
Current programme: African Nature Futures Lab / FLOURISH
Recognition: Inaugural African Planet Prize, 2026

title: Rohini Pande: Can institutions redistribute economic and environmental power?
text:
Rohini Pande is the Henry J. Heinz II Professor of Economics at Yale University, Director of the Economic Growth Center and Faculty Director of Inclusion Economics. Her research asks how institutions shape who has political, economic and environmental power. Yale describes her work as focused on the ways formal and informal institutions determine patterns of advantage in low- and middle-income countries.
Pande trained in economics in Delhi, philosophy, politics and economics at Oxford, and completed a PhD in economics at the London School of Economics. Before Yale she was a professor at Harvard Kennedy School, where she helped build Evidence for Policy Design. Across that career, field experiments and policy partnerships have been used to test institutional reforms rather than only describe inequality.
Her work spans gender, political representation, digital governance and environmental regulation. Recent research in India has examined pollution markets, payments for ecosystem services and the design of state programmes. A 2025 Quarterly Journal of Economics paper evaluated the world’s first cap-and-trade market for particulate pollution in Gujarat and found that emissions trading could reduce pollution while lowering compliance costs.
The common thread is institutional design. Markets, quotas, digital systems and local government rules are not neutral delivery mechanisms. They change who receives information, who can enforce rights and who bears costs. Pande’s research treats those rules as objects that can be tested empirically.
The unresolved question is scale and durability. A reform can work in an experiment or one state and still fail when political incentives change. Pande’s work therefore asks whether institutions can be designed not only to produce a measurable short-term effect but to alter power relationships strongly enough that gains persist.

Rohini Pande

title: Research context: FUSION and FORESIGHT
text:
FORESIGHT project illustration, FUSION, University of Galway, used under CC BY-SA 4.0.


Much of what I write here about Irish agriculture and climate policy comes from inside a government-funded modelling programme, and readers should know that before they read the rest.
I am doing my PhD within FUSION, the FUture Sustainable economy Integrated mOdelling Network at the University of Galway. The group works across life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment, land-use modelling and environmental software. In practice a question about agriculture does not have to stay inside an agricultural model. It can lead into forestry, energy, emissions accounting or land allocation.
Much of my work also sits alongside FORESIGHT, a project funded by Ireland’s Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications under a services contract to provide agriculture and land-use modelling to the Climate Action Modelling Group. FUSION leads the project with the University of Limerick and FERS Ltd. So when I write about Irish climate, agriculture or land-use policy, I am writing as someone who works inside a programme connected to those subjects. The views are my own and do not represent the University of Galway, the Department, funders or collaborators.
One of the tools in this environment is GOBLIN, which links agriculture, forestry and other land uses within a national land-balance framework. My own questions mostly begin after a national pathway has been made internally coherent. A national result can say that livestock, forestry or another land use changes by a given amount, but that change eventually has to meet a geography and a population of farms that differ from one another. The same national adjustment looks quite different when it reaches dairy, beef or other systems in different parts of the country. A model can be consistent in aggregate and still leave open where the transition falls, who carries it, and whether the land implied by several objectives can fit in the same places.
The habit I value most in this group is treating models as things to question. Assumptions should be visible enough to change, alternatives easy enough to test, and every result should arrive with some sense of what the model cannot tell us. Written down, that sounds like common sense. It becomes much harder to practise once a model is large and technically impressive.
The site will range well beyond my PhD, into economics, technology, Ghana, Ireland, the United States, books and code. When a post touches Irish agriculture or climate policy, though, this is the background I want readers to keep in mind.

Elvis Kwame Ofori

title: BioLand-US
text:
Energy-crop models can say where perennial biomass could be grown in the United States. They cannot say whether farmers will sign up. BioLand-US sits between those two things and asks a practical implementation question:

When a techno-economic model allocates land to perennial biomass, how much of that prospective allocation can also be supported by compatible agricultural land and voluntary contractual participation?

The model does not replace or re-optimise the upstream resource allocation. It adds an explicit implementation layer.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Ireland’s national plans for agriculture and land use can say how much livestock numbers fall and how much land changes use. They do not say where. GOBLIN-Spatial is about the where.
National AFOLU (agriculture, forestry and other land use) pathways can specify how livestock numbers, land release and future land uses change without showing where those changes fall.
GOBLIN-Spatial asks:

When a nationally coherent agricultural transition requires restructuring, where does transition pressure concentrate, what can the released land support, and can competing future land-use requirements be accommodated within the available geography?

GOBLIN supplies the national pathway. GOBLIN-Spatial resolves its geography and tests spatial feasibility.

text:
How it works





flowchart TD
    A["National GOBLIN pathway"] --> B["Transition incidence<br/>Where does adjustment fall?"]
    B --> C["Spatial response potential<br/>What can released land support?"]
    C --> D["Spatial transformability<br/>Can competing future land uses fit?"]
    D --> E["Spatial flexibility<br/>Is one geography necessary?"]






The framework is a spatial stress-test of transition pathways, not a prediction of individual farmer or parcel decisions.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Evidence and scale
The historical reconstruction covers 2015–2025 and is anchored to the 2020 Census of Agriculture at Electoral Division level. Higher-level livestock controls maintain national accounting consistency while preserving validated local structure.
The model combines agricultural statistics with land, soil and drainage information, LPIS context and explicit eligibility controls.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
What it does not claim
The model does not predict individual farmer behaviour, household welfare, market prices, parcel-level adoption or the exact geography that will exist in 2050.
Those questions require behavioural, farm-level or market models.
